\begin{abstract}
Large language models stream their responses token by token, so a response cannot be signed as a whole
before its first byte is sent. With post-quantum signatures this matters: an ML-DSA-65 signature is
3,309\,B against $\approx$71\,B for ECDSA. We measure the resulting trade-off with PQ-Shield, an
application-layer emulation of protected inference transactions (not a TLS implementation), on a real
Llama-3.2-3B backend. Treating per-chunk and hash-chained signing as the endpoints of a hash chain
checkpointed every $k$ chunks, we measure signature bytes against \emph{exposure}, the tokens a client
displays before a verified signature covers them: from 135,669\,B and 5 tokens at $k{=}1$ to 3,309\,B and the
whole 200-token response at $k{=}\infty$, with byte counts that match an analytic model exactly.
Per-signature time inside a stream reaches up to 18$\times$ a back-to-back microbenchmark, because the
processor slows between chunks; we bound it rather than predict it. Binding role, session, and position into
every signed message, a signed end-of-stream record, and client enforcement of the requested checkpoint
schedule detected every one of 135,000 trials of static and adaptive attacks across six
configurations, with no false rejections in 750 genuine streams; without the schedule check, stripping
checkpoints went undetected in all 9,000 trials. Detection, however, arrives only with a signature,
and $k$ bounds how much unverified text was shown by then. Against an unauthenticated handshake, key
substitution succeeded in all 1,800 trials regardless of post-quantum primitives; a transcript signature
under a pinned identity key stopped all 3,600 attempts at no resolvable latency cost. Key-establishment
results, measured with a matched no-crypto protocol control on a single host, confirm prior TLS
studies: at 10 connections, ML-KEM configurations add 1.3--5.4\,ms of cryptographic overhead per
92\,ms transaction and are equivalent to X25519 within $\pm5\%$. Our ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 bindings
reproduce all 130 tested NIST ACVP vectors, including ML-DSA key generation and signing.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
post-quantum cryptography, ML-DSA, ML-KEM, stream authentication, LLM streaming, hybrid key exchange,
harvest-now-decrypt-later, inference APIs, measurement
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
AI inference endpoints---hosted by commercial providers, on managed cloud platforms, or as custom
FastAPI/Flask services---carry model inputs and outputs that can be sensitive: diagnostic features,
financial records, and increasingly the full text of conversational and agentic sessions. Inference
endpoints are already a recognised attack surface for interception, tampering, and privacy leakage
\cite{tidjon2022threat,song2019privacy}. Their transport protection rests on RSA or elliptic-curve
key exchange and signatures, all of which Shor's algorithm breaks in polynomial time on a
sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer~\cite{shor1997}. Such a machine does not yet
exist, but the harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) threat means an adversary can record encrypted
traffic today and decrypt it once one does; data whose confidentiality must outlive the arrival of a
CRQC is already exposed~\cite{mosca2018ready,blancoromero2026hndl}.

NIST finalized its first post-quantum standards in August 2024: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key
encapsulation~\cite{fips203} and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for signatures~\cite{fips204}. Protocol-level
migration is under way---the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid group is already negotiated by major browsers and
content-delivery networks~\cite{ietf-ecdhe-mlkem}---and post-quantum TLS has been benchmarked
extensively~\cite{paquin2020benchmarking,sikeridis2020authentication,montenegro2026framework,gomezcambronero2026layered}.
For key establishment, that literature has largely settled the cost question: post-quantum key
exchange adds little computation, and its larger messages matter mainly on slow or lossy links. Less
is known about \emph{signatures} on responses that are streamed. A large language model (LLM)
returns its answer token by token, so the response cannot be signed as a whole before the first byte
is sent. Signing every chunk is then the obvious design, and with a post-quantum signature it is an
expensive one: an ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309\,B against $\approx$71\,B for ECDSA P-256. Amortizing
one signature over many chunks is a classical idea~\cite{gennaro1997streams,wong1999flows,perrig2000tesla},
but it trades bytes for a window in which the client shows text no signature yet covers. How large
that window is, what it costs, and how an adversary can exploit it have not, to our knowledge, been
measured for post-quantum signatures on LLM streams.

This paper is a measurement study of that trade-off, carried out with PQ-Shield, an application-layer
emulation of protected inference transactions (not a TLS implementation). Its contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{The signature schedule as the post-quantum cost of streaming.} On a real
  Llama-3.2-3B backend, we treat per-chunk and hash-chained signing as the endpoints of one design
  space---a hash chain checkpointed every $k$ chunks---define \emph{exposure} (the tokens a client
  displays before a verified signature covers them), and measure signature bytes, exposure, and
  verification lag for $k\in\{1,2,5,10,20,\infty\}$. Signature counts and bytes match an analytic model
  exactly; we also explain why per-signature \emph{time} inside a stream exceeds microbenchmarks.
  \item \emph{Stream integrity under static and adaptive attack.} We show that naive per-chunk signing
  admits undetected truncation, fix it by binding role, session, and position into every signed
  message and ending each stream with a signed length record, and evaluate drop, reorder,
  duplication, replay, truncation, whole-session replay, and five attacks that target checkpoints
  (500 trials per cell, with confidence bounds and a false-rejection baseline). One adaptive
  attack---stripping checkpoints---defeats a client that does not enforce the checkpoint schedule it
  requested; we close it.
  \item \emph{The adversary an unauthenticated handshake invites.} A key-substitution attack against a
  live server succeeds against the unauthenticated handshake every time and fails every time once the
  client checks a transcript signature under a pinned identity key, whose cost we measure.
  \item \emph{Key establishment, as confirmation.} Seven configurations---including an X25519 baseline,
  the deployed X25519MLKEM768 hybrid, its combination with ML-DSA-65, and a matched no-crypto protocol
  control---under concurrency (10--1,000 connections), four payload shapes, byte-level network
  emulation, and session reuse, analyzed with repetition-level statistics. These results confirm, in an
  inference setting, what the post-quantum TLS literature found for generic traffic.
  \item \emph{Ground truth.} Our ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 bindings reproduce all 130 tested NIST ACVP
  known-answer vectors, including ML-DSA-65 key generation and signing byte for byte.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Background and Related Work}

\subsection{Post-Quantum Primitives}
ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203) is a module-lattice key-encapsulation mechanism at NIST security category 3,
with public key, secret key, and ciphertext sizes of 1,184, 2,400, and 1,088 bytes and a 32-byte
shared secret. ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) is a module-lattice signature scheme at the same category, with
public key, secret key, and signature sizes of 1,952, 4,032, and 3,309 bytes. Several publications
that post-date FIPS~204 still quote pre-standardization CRYSTALS-Dilithium3 values (a 3,293-byte
signature and 4,000-byte secret key); all values in this paper are confirmed against FIPS~204 as
finalized (Section~\ref{sec:validation}). The X25519MLKEM768 hybrid~\cite{ietf-ecdhe-mlkem}
concatenates an ML-KEM-768 share with a 32-byte X25519 share and derives the session key from both
shared secrets, so it stays secure unless both algorithms are broken.

\subsection{Related Work}
Table~\ref{tab:related_work} synthesizes fifteen studies spanning heterogeneous-hardware PQC
benchmarking, industry deployment, layered TLS 1.3 evaluation, migration surveys, 5G/6G integration,
ML threat modeling, and HNDL economics. Among the studies we reviewed, we found none that measures
post-quantum signatures on streamed model responses, and none that evaluates migration with AI
inference payloads under load together with adversarial experiments; we do not claim this survey is
exhaustive. Three further lines of work bear directly on our design.

\paragraph*{Post-quantum TLS under network conditions}
Paquin \emph{et al.}~\cite{paquin2020benchmarking} benchmarked post-quantum key exchange and
signatures inside TLS 1.3 over emulated links (Linux \texttt{netem}), showing that on lossy or
low-bandwidth paths message size, not computation, dominates handshake latency. Sikeridis
\emph{et al.}~\cite{sikeridis2020authentication} reached a similar conclusion for post-quantum
authentication, and Montenegro \emph{et al.}~\cite{montenegro2026framework} and
G\'omez-Cambronero \emph{et al.}~\cite{gomezcambronero2026layered} extend the analysis to layered TLS
and application-level load. These works measure the TLS handshake with generic payloads. PQ-Shield
instead measures an application-layer protocol around AI inference payloads, including streaming
responses, and adds controlled adversarial experiments. Our network emulation
(Section~\ref{sec:netem}) is deliberately coarser than theirs---it shapes the byte stream rather than
packets---and we use it to bound, not replace, their packet-level results.

\paragraph*{Stream authentication}
Signing a stream that is not available in full when transmission starts is a classical problem.
Gennaro and Rohatgi~\cite{gennaro1997streams} chain per-block hashes so that one signature
authenticates an entire stream; Wong and Lam~\cite{wong1999flows} amortize one signature over a flow
with hash trees; TESLA and EMSS~\cite{perrig2000tesla} trade immediate verification for low
per-packet overhead. Our hash-chain strategy is an instance of this family, not a new construction,
and inherits the same trade-off: integrity is confirmed only when a signature arrives. What is new is
the setting. LLM token streams have a small, latency-critical first chunk and, with post-quantum
signatures, a per-signature cost large enough that the choice of amortization decides whether
streaming is affordable at all; we make that choice explicit and measurable through checkpointing
(Section~\ref{sec:checkpoint}).

\paragraph*{Side channels in encrypted LLM streams}
Weiss \emph{et al.}~\cite{weiss2024keylogging} recovered the content of encrypted AI-assistant
responses from the sizes of streamed packets (the token-length side channel). The attack is
orthogonal to the key exchange and applies to every protected configuration here, but it sharpens one
qualification: per-chunk and hash-chained signing emit one record per chunk and therefore expose
chunk count and timing, which only buffer-and-sign hides.

\section{Threat Model}\label{sec:threats}

\subsection{Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL)}
A passive adversary records every cryptographic artifact on a protected connection---the
key-establishment blob, every AES-256-GCM (nonce, ciphertext) pair, and any signatures---and stores
them until a CRQC becomes available. We assume AES-256-GCM itself remains secure (Grover's algorithm
only halves its effective key length), so what differs between configurations is whether the recorded
handshake lets the adversary recover the session key. Under Shor's algorithm this holds for
RSA-OAEP and X25519. For ML-KEM-768 and X25519MLKEM768 it does not under currently known quantum
attacks, assuming a correct implementation. This is a statement about the modeled key-recovery attack
on the recorded handshake, not a proof that the protocol resists every future attack. The quantity we
measure is the \emph{byte volume} that becomes decryptable, not its information content; note also that
response lengths already leak through packet sizes without any quantum computer~\cite{weiss2024keylogging},
so the incremental harm of HNDL is the plaintext content itself.

\subsection{Active Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)}
We consider two active adversaries. The first \emph{tampers} with protected records in transit---it
flips a bit in the AEAD ciphertext or in the signature---without touching the handshake; this tests
whether, where, and how quickly the client's checks reject modified data. The second is the adversary
an \emph{unauthenticated} handshake invites: it replaces the server's key shares and signing key with
its own, terminates both legs, reads the request, and re-signs a response of its choosing. No
signature or AEAD check can stop this, because the client verifies under whatever key it was given.
By default PQ-Shield's handshake is unauthenticated, like an anonymous key exchange; we measure the
key-substitution attack against it and against an \emph{authenticated} variant in which the server
signs the handshake transcript with a long-term identity key the client has pinned
(Section~\ref{sec:auth}), playing the role of a certificate and CertificateVerify in TLS~1.3. All
latency experiments use the unauthenticated handshake unless stated otherwise.

\subsection{Streaming-Specific Threats}
Two threats appear only when one connection streams many chunks. The first is a
\emph{sequence-integrity attack}, in which an on-path adversary rearranges validly protected records
without forging any: it may drop a chunk, reorder two chunks, duplicate a chunk, substitute a validly
signed chunk recorded from \emph{another} session (cross-session replay), or truncate the stream by
cutting it off before its last chunks and its terminal record (forged termination). Each chunk's AEAD
tag and, under naive per-chunk signing, its signature remain valid, so detection requires binding
every signed message to its role, its session, and its position, and authenticating the end of the
stream. Our protocol binds a 3-byte role label, a 32-byte session context derived from the handshake
identifier (one stream per handshake, so it also identifies the stream), and the chunk index into
every signed message, and ends every stream with a signed record that commits to the number of chunks
(Section~\ref{sec:binding}). We measure how early each strategy detects each attack.

The second is \emph{HNDL exposure that compounds with session length}. A streamed session reuses one
session key for every chunk, so a passive adversary who records the handshake captures the whole
session at once: the longer the stream, the more ciphertext becomes retroactively readable the moment
the key exchange is broken. We quantify this by relating the number of generated tokens to the
volume a single future key recovery would expose. None of the evaluated configurations rotates keys
within a session; mid-stream rekeying is left to future work.

\section{System Design}\label{sec:design}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{system_overview.pdf}
\caption{PQ-Shield architecture. Separate server processes wrap the same FastAPI inference service: an
unprotected control (also used, with an extra no-crypto request, as Control-2RT) and six protected
configurations that share the handshake/predict endpoints,
the AES-256-GCM + HKDF-SHA256 session layer, and one \texttt{ServerCryptoConfig} contract, so only the
key-establishment and signature primitives differ. ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 come from a
\texttt{ctypes} binding to liboqs; RSA, X25519, and ECDSA from OpenSSL via the Python
\texttt{cryptography} package.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure*}

PQ-Shield is an \emph{application-layer emulation of protected inference transactions}, not an
implementation of TLS: it reproduces the cryptographic work of key establishment, payload encryption,
and response signing around an inference call, without certificate authentication or TLS framing.
Separate processes wrap the same FastAPI inference server (Fig.~\ref{fig:architecture}): an
unprotected control and six protected configurations (Table~\ref{tab:configs}) sharing a common
\texttt{ServerCryptoConfig}/\texttt{ClientCryptoConfig} contract, so that only the asymmetric
key-establishment and signature primitives differ. All protected configurations use the same
AES-256-GCM layer keyed by HKDF-SHA256 over the raw shared secret. Every protected transaction follows
the same five steps---handshake, session-key establishment, encrypt-and-send, decrypt, verify
(Fig.~\ref{fig:sequence})---with a fresh ephemeral key pair per transaction by default.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Configurations. ECDSA is over P-256; ``PQ'': key exchange resists a CRQC. All protected configurations share AES-256-GCM with an HKDF-SHA256 session key.}
\label{tab:configs}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}lL{2.6cm}lc@{}}
\toprule
Configuration & Key establishment & Signature & PQ \\
\midrule
Control & none & none & -- \\
A: Classical-RSA & RSA-2048-OAEP (new key per handshake) & ECDSA & no \\
A$'$: Classical-ECDHE & ephemeral X25519 & ECDSA & no \\
B: Hybrid & ML-KEM-768 & ECDSA & yes \\
B$'$: Hybrid-KEX & X25519MLKEM768 & ECDSA & yes \\
C: Full PQC & ML-KEM-768 & ML-DSA-65 & yes \\
C$'$: Hybrid-KEX-PQ & X25519MLKEM768 & ML-DSA-65 & yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Configuration A$'$ is an X25519-based classical baseline representative of the key-establishment
primitive used in modern TLS deployments: TLS 1.3 removed RSA key transport~\cite{rfc8446}, and
ephemeral X25519 is the classical half of the X25519MLKEM768 group now negotiated on the
web~\cite{ietf-ecdhe-mlkem}. A$'$ and B have identical signature code, so
A$'\!\rightarrow$B isolates exactly one change, X25519 to ML-KEM-768. Configuration A uses RSA-2048-OAEP key transport with per-transaction key
generation; no production system generates RSA keys per handshake, so we include A as a legacy
worst-case baseline that exposes the cost of RSA key generation under load, not as \emph{the}
classical baseline. Configuration B pairs a post-quantum key exchange (ML-KEM-768 alone) with a classical
signature. Configuration B$'$ instead combines X25519 and ML-KEM-768 \emph{within} the key exchange,
following~\cite{ietf-ecdhe-mlkem}: the server's share is the ML-KEM encapsulation key followed by an
X25519 public key (1,216\,B), the client's is the ML-KEM ciphertext followed by its X25519 public key
(1,120\,B), and the session key is derived from both shared secrets concatenated. With identical
signature code, A$'\!\rightarrow$B$'$ is the migration step deployed on the web today, and
B$\rightarrow$B$'$ the price of hedging against an ML-KEM break. Configuration C$'$ combines B$'$'s key
exchange with C's ML-DSA-65 signatures: post-quantum on both axes and hedged in the key exchange. It
was added in revision and is measured in the concurrency, streaming, checkpoint, threat, and
authentication experiments, but not in the payload, network, and session-reuse sweeps.

\paragraph*{Authenticated handshake (optional)}\label{sec:auth}
In the default handshake nothing binds the key shares to the server. In the authenticated variant
(enabled per server), the server holds a long-term identity key---ECDSA P-256 for configurations that
sign with ECDSA, ML-DSA-65 for C and C$'$, so a post-quantum configuration stays post-quantum---and
returns, with every handshake, a signature over
$\text{SHA-256}(\texttt{"PQ-Shield-handshake-v1"}\parallel\texttt{0x00}\parallel\mathit{hid}\parallel
\mathit{alg}_{\mathrm{kex}}\parallel\mathit{alg}_{\mathrm{sig}}\parallel\mathit{pk}_{\mathrm{kex}}\parallel\mathit{pk}_{\mathrm{sig}})$,
with each field length-prefixed. The client pins the identity public key once, out of band (in our
harness, from a dedicated endpoint before any measured transaction, standing in for a certificate it
already trusts), and rejects any handshake whose transcript signature does not verify. We do not
model a PKI or certificate chains.

Streaming experiments use a real Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model (Q4\_K\_M, llama.cpp with Metal). The
concurrency, payload-shape, network, session-reuse, HNDL, and MITM experiments use the non-streaming
endpoint with a RandomForest classifier (or the selected payload profile). One locally hosted LLM
produces $\approx$40 tokens per second for a single stream, so a 1,000-connection LLM sweep would
measure the model's queue rather than the cryptography.

\section{Methodology}

\subsection{Environment and Process Isolation}
All measurements were taken on one host (Apple M3 MacBook Air, 8 cores, 16\,GB, macOS) on AC power
with low-power mode disabled, on a single day. Each configuration's server runs in its own process,
is health-checked, swept, and stopped before the next configuration starts, so no two configurations
share the CPU. All endpoints, including the control's, run their request handlers in the server's
worker thread pool, so the control is not disadvantaged by blocking inference on the event loop.
Every sweep records a run identifier, the host, and its parameters with each raw row, and the
analysis uses each configuration's most recent run.

\subsection{Cryptographic Binding and Protocol Construction}
ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 are accessed through a purpose-built \texttt{ctypes} binding against a
locally compiled liboqs~\cite{stebila2016oqs} rather than the higher-level \texttt{liboqs-python}
wrapper. The binding exposes the six C entry points the configurations use (key generation,
encapsulation, and decapsulation for ML-KEM-768; key generation, signing, and verification for
ML-DSA-65), plus, for validation only, context-string signing and liboqs's hook for replacing its
random-number source (Section~\ref{sec:validation}), with byte
lengths asserted against the FIPS~203/204 constants at every call boundary, so a build or linkage
error surfaces immediately rather than propagating malformed key material. liboqs is compiled with
only these two algorithms, which keeps continuous re-verification of the binding
(Section~\ref{sec:validation}) cheap. RSA-OAEP, X25519, ECDSA P-256, and AES-256-GCM come from OpenSSL
through the Python \texttt{cryptography} package.

The handshake orchestration, AES-256-GCM payload encryption (keyed by HKDF-SHA256 over the raw shared
secret in every configuration, including Classical-RSA's OAEP-transported key), and FastAPI plumbing
are identical code paths across configurations, so differences between them can be attributed to the
asymmetric primitives. By default a fresh ephemeral key pair is generated on every transaction---the
conservative worst case; Section~\ref{sec:sessions} measures the amortized case.

\paragraph*{Stream message binding}\label{sec:binding}
For streaming, the same signature primitive is applied to strategy-specific messages, each beginning
with a 3-byte role label and the session context
$\mathit{ctx}=\text{SHA-256}(\texttt{"PQ-Shield-stream-v2"}\parallel\texttt{0x00}\parallel\mathit{hid})$,
where $\mathit{hid}$ is the handshake identifier and $i$, $n$ are 4-byte big-endian integers:
\begin{itemize}
  \item buffer-and-sign: $\mathrm{Sign}(\texttt{BUF}\parallel\mathit{ctx}\parallel\text{nonce}\parallel\text{ct})$;
  \item per-chunk: $\mathrm{Sign}(\texttt{CHK}\parallel\mathit{ctx}\parallel i\parallel\text{nonce}\parallel\text{ct}_i)$
  for every chunk, then a terminal $\mathrm{Sign}(\texttt{END}\parallel\mathit{ctx}\parallel n)$;
  \item hash-chain: $h_0=\text{SHA-256}(\texttt{GEN}\parallel\mathit{ctx})$,
  \begin{equation}
  h_i = \text{SHA-256}(h_{i-1} \parallel i \parallel \text{nonce}_i \parallel \text{ct}_i),
  \end{equation}
  optional checkpoints $\mathrm{Sign}(\texttt{CKP}\parallel\mathit{ctx}\parallel i\parallel h_i)$,
  and a terminal $\mathrm{Sign}(\texttt{FIN}\parallel\mathit{ctx}\parallel n\parallel h_n)$.
\end{itemize}
The role label separates the five message types; $\mathit{ctx}$ makes a record signed for one session
fail verification in any other, even if a server reused one long-term signing key (ours are
per-handshake, which also prevents it); the index binds position; and the terminal records commit to
the stream length. The client requires the terminal record, checks its count against the chunks it
accepted, and recomputes $h_i$ itself rather than trusting transmitted chain hashes.

\subsection{Concurrency Benchmark}
Load is generated by an asynchronous client with a bounded worker pool, so the achieved concurrency
matches the requested level as latency varies. Besides the control (one unprotected request per
transaction) we run a \emph{matched-protocol control}, Control-2RT, which makes the same two HTTP
requests as a protected transaction---a handshake request and the inference request---with no
cryptographic work. Protected minus Control-2RT is then the cryptographic overhead alone, and
Control-2RT minus control the protocol overhead of the extra round trip. Each cell (configuration $\times$ concurrency
$\times$ repetition) sends ten requests per connection (with a floor for low concurrency), and five
repetitions are collected at 10, 100, and 1,000 connections. The first 5\% of requests in each cell
are discarded as warm-up. Latency is end-to-end (\texttt{total\_ms}: handshake round trip plus
protected request), the only quantity directly comparable to the control's single request. A sampler records server CPU and resident memory every 0.25\,s.
Failed requests are counted, classified by stage (handshake or protected request) and cause, and
excluded from latency statistics; because failure rates differ between configurations, we repeat
every comparison at the levels where failures occur with each failed request counted at the 30\,s
client timeout, slower than any successful request (Section~\ref{sec:res-concurrency}).

\paragraph*{Statistical design} Requests within one repetition share a server process, its warm-up
state, and its queue, so they are not independent; the \emph{repetition} is our unit of analysis. We
report the median, p95, failure rate, and the range of the five per-repetition medians. Differences
between configurations are differences in medians with 95\% confidence intervals from a two-stage
bootstrap (1,000 draws: resample repetitions, then requests within each drawn repetition). Effect
sizes are Cliff's $\delta$. Significance uses the two-sided Mann--Whitney $U$ test on per-repetition
medians (five versus five, so the smallest attainable $p$ is 0.008), Holm-corrected within each
family of comparisons against one reference at one concurrency level. To support claims that two configurations perform the same, we test
equivalence with two one-sided tests: a configuration is declared equivalent to a reference when
the 90\% bootstrap CI of the median difference lies within $\pm5\%$ of the reference median. We call
a difference \emph{practically significant} only if its CI excludes a 5\% band, not merely zero.

\subsection{Payload-Shape Sensitivity}
Four profiles are swept at 10 connections with the control and the five original protected
configurations (five repetitions):
\texttt{tabular\_small} (a 100-tree RandomForest trained on the UCI handwritten-digits dataset,
345\,B request / 93\,B response), \texttt{image\_cnn} (a fixed-weight NumPy convolutional network on a
synthetic $32\times32\times3$ image, 4,138\,B / 244\,B), \texttt{embedding} (a synthetic 768-dimension
vector generator, 202\,B / 8,022\,B), and \texttt{llm\_completion} (a synthetic text generator,
163\,B request). The synthetic profiles probe payload shape and size; they are not claims of
representative model behaviour.

\subsection{Streaming Signature Strategies}
The streaming endpoint sends chunks as Server-Sent Events over one HTTP response; each event carries
one strategy-specific record (nonce, ciphertext, and, depending on strategy, a signature and/or chain
hash). The model's blocking token generator is bridged into the server's event loop through a worker
thread so that generation does not stall other requests. Time to first token (TTFT) is measured at
the client from issuing the request to receiving the first event. Each configuration $\times$ strategy
$\times$ length cell (50 and 200 tokens, 5-token chunks) has ten repetitions; after each server start
one discarded generation absorbs the model's cold start, and the order of cells is shuffled with a
fixed seed so that no strategy is always measured first.

\paragraph*{Timing signatures inside a stream} Every signing and verification call records both
wall-clock time and the calling thread's CPU time. The two differ when the thread waits---for the CPU or
for Python's interpreter lock while the model's token loop runs in another thread---so CPU time isolates
the work of the operation itself. A separate diagnostic times 300 back-to-back calls and 100 calls spaced
125\,ms apart (one 5-token chunk at $\approx$40 tokens/s), each with the CPU idle and while Llama generates
in the same process, to relate in-stream costs to microbenchmarks (Section~\ref{sec:timing}).

\subsection{Checkpointed Hash Chains and Exposure}\label{sec:checkpoint}
The hash-chain strategy can additionally sign the running digest $h_i$ every $k$ chunks. The client
verifies each checkpoint signature against its \emph{own} recomputed $h_i$, so any dropped, reordered,
or altered chunk before a checkpoint makes that checkpoint fail mid-stream. For an $n$-chunk response
this costs $\lfloor n/k\rfloor + 1$ signatures (checkpoints plus the terminal one), and a decrypted
chunk waits at most $k$ chunks for coverage. We record two exposure measures per transaction: the
largest number of chunks displayed but not yet covered by a verified signature (\emph{max unverified
chunks}), and the longest time any chunk waited for coverage (\emph{verification lag}). Per-chunk
signing is the $k{=}1$ endpoint (exposure one chunk) and plain hash-chain the $k{=}\infty$ endpoint
(exposure the whole response). We sweep $k\in\{1,2,5,10,20,\infty\}$ for Hybrid (71\,B signatures), Full
PQC, and Hybrid-KEX-PQ (3,309\,B) on 200-token Llama responses in 5-token chunks (five repetitions).
Because the client requested $k$, it knows where checkpoints must appear and treats a missing one as a
failure; Section~\ref{sec:res-campaign} shows why this check is needed.

\subsection{Session Resumption}\label{sec:sessions}
To measure the amortized case, a client may set \texttt{keep\_session}: the server then caches the
derived session key under the handshake identifier, later requests carry no key-establishment blob
and reuse it, and the last request of the session ends it. Each of 10 concurrent clients reuses one
key exchange for $N\in\{1,10,100\}$ requests (1,000 requests per cell, five repetitions), and we report
end-to-end overhead against the control.

\subsection{Network Emulation}\label{sec:netem}
All other experiments run over loopback, where moving an extra 1,088-byte ML-KEM ciphertext or
3,309-byte ML-DSA signature costs almost nothing. To expose the cost of message size we place a TCP
proxy between load generator and server that adds a one-way propagation delay of RTT/2 in each
direction and a per-direction bottleneck bandwidth shared by all connections; bytes are released in
order, so HTTP semantics are unchanged. We evaluate four paths---loopback, \emph{metro} (10\,ms RTT,
100\,Mbit/s), \emph{WAN} (50\,ms, 20\,Mbit/s), and \emph{mobile} (100\,ms, 5\,Mbit/s)---each with the control
and the five original protected configurations at 10 connections and five repetitions. The proxy shapes the byte stream above TCP; it
does not model slow start, the initial congestion window, loss, or fragmentation, all of which
penalize large handshakes further~\cite{paquin2020benchmarking}, so the measured cost is a lower
bound.

\subsection{Threat Injection}
For HNDL, the server reports, behind a debug header that does not alter ordinary traffic, the exact
size of each cryptographic artifact it sends (1,000 transactions per configuration). We distinguish
\emph{harvestable} bytes, everything a passive adversary captures (key-establishment blob, AEAD
records, signatures, chain hashes), from \emph{decryptable} bytes, the encrypted application-payload
records whose plaintext becomes recoverable once the session key is recovered. For a stream of $n$
chunks,
\begin{equation}
D = \mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{KEX}}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(|\text{nonce}_i| + |\text{ct}_i|\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{KEX}}$ is 1 if a CRQC can recover the session key from the recorded handshake
(RSA-OAEP, X25519) and 0 otherwise (ML-KEM-768, X25519MLKEM768), $|\text{nonce}_i|=12$\,B and $\text{ct}_i$ includes the 16-byte GCM tag; the recoverable
plaintext is $D-28n$ bytes. Signatures, public keys, and chain hashes are excluded from $D$: they are
not secret. One session key protects the whole stream, and each 5-token chunk is one AEAD record, so
$D$ per token depends on the chunk size (framing) and on the tokenizer (plaintext). For streaming, response length is varied with the
configuration and strategy held fixed, so exposure can be attributed to length alone.

For tampering, a minimal forward proxy flips one bit in either the ciphertext or the signature field of
each response (100 responses per configuration and target). The client decrypts before verifying, and
detection time is the duration of the rejecting step itself---the AEAD tag check or the signature
verification---so the two defence layers are directly comparable.

\paragraph*{Stream-integrity campaign} For each protected configuration and each of five cells
(per-chunk; hash chain with $k=\infty$, 10, 5, 2) we capture a pool of ten real 100-token Llama streams
from a live server, verify each unmodified (false rejections), and run 500 trials per attack, each on a
random pool stream at a random position, through the client's incremental verification---the same checks
the streaming client makes. Whether an attack is detected is a deterministic function of the captured
stream and the attack position, so trials sample streams and positions rather than repeat network
events. Static attacks are drop, reorder, duplicate, replay of a chunk from another session, truncation
at a random point (losing the terminal record), and replay of an entire other session. Adaptive attacks,
for checkpointed chains, strip every checkpoint signature, move a checkpoint signature to the next chunk,
drop the chunk just before or just after a checkpoint, and swap a checkpoint chunk with its successor.
For each detected attack we record whether it was caught before the stream ended and how many chunks
the client had displayed with no verified signature covering them at that moment. Rates carry exact
(Clopper--Pearson) 95\% intervals.

\paragraph*{Key substitution} Against a live server with the authenticated variant enabled, an
in-process adversary sits between the client's messages and the server: it substitutes its own key
shares and signing key (keeping the server's transcript signature, or re-signing the transcript with its
own identity key), or relays the handshake and flips a response bit. Each variant runs 300 times per
configuration against a client that ignores the transcript signature and one that checks it under the
pinned key, with an unattacked baseline; we record acceptance, whether the adversary read the request,
and whether a forged prediction was accepted.

\subsection{Ground-Truth Validation}
Two independent validations correspond to the two ways this paper's results could be wrong. First,
the primitive bindings are checked against official NIST Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol
(ACVP) known-answer tests~\cite{acvp} by
re-deriving each vector's output from its input and comparing byte for byte. liboqs exposes
derandomized ML-KEM functions but no derandomized ML-DSA key generation or signing; however, every
random byte its ML-DSA code consumes comes from one replaceable source. FIPS~204 key generation draws
exactly the 32-byte seed $\xi$ and signing exactly the 32-byte $\mathit{rnd}$ (zero for deterministic
signing), so we substitute a source that returns the vector's bytes and check that liboqs drew exactly
those bytes and no more. This exercises the same entry points the configurations call. Second, because no
external dataset exists for streaming signature overhead, the streaming harness is checked against an
analytic model: signature count and bytes follow deterministically from the number of chunks and the
strategy (one signature for buffer-and-sign and plain hash-chain, one per chunk for per-chunk,
$\lfloor n/k\rfloor+1$ for checkpointed hash-chain), and signing time follows from the count and the
independently measured per-signature cost.

\subsection{Reproducibility and Artifact Availability}
Every sweep records its run identifier, host, and parameters with each raw row. The software
environment (OS and package versions, OpenSSL and liboqs revisions, the SHA-256 of the model files,
and the repository commit) is captured automatically at run time and listed in
Table~\ref{tab:environment}. Code, configuration, result summaries, and the scripts that regenerate
every figure and table are released at
\url{https://github.com/Yuvicodes1/PQ-Shield-Benchmarking-Post-Quantum-Security-for-AI-APIs}.

% =============================================================================
\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

We report the streaming results first, because they carry the paper's main finding, and then the
key-establishment results, which confirm prior TLS work in this setting.

\subsection{Streaming Signature Strategies}\label{sec:res-streaming}
With the real Llama-3.2-3B backend (Fig.~\ref{fig:streaming}, Table~\ref{tab:streaming}),
buffer-and-sign delays the first token to the end of generation (5.0--5.5\,s for a 200-token response).
Per-chunk and hash-chain signing deliver the first token in 126--139\,ms, 40--43$\times$ sooner, in
every configuration. The strategies differ in signature bytes: with ML-DSA-65 (Full PQC and
Hybrid-KEX-PQ) a 200-token response carries 135,669\,B of signatures under per-chunk signing (40 chunk
signatures plus the signed end record) versus 3,309\,B under hash-chain, a 41$\times$ difference; with
ECDSA the corresponding figures are $\approx$2,910\,B and 71\,B. All 360 streams verified completely. Strategy
order was shuffled within each configuration, so comparisons between strategies are unbiased;
generation speed drifted over the sweep (thermal throttling of the fanless host), so we do not compare
streaming times between configurations.

error bars interquartile range). (a, c) Time to first token: per-chunk and hash-chain deliver the
first token about 40$\times$ sooner than buffer-and-sign. (b, d) Signature bytes per response:
per-chunk ML-DSA-65 signing costs 41$\times$ the bytes of hash-chain.}

\subsection{Bounded Exposure with Checkpointed Hash Chains}\label{sec:res-checkpoint}
Fig.~\ref{fig:checkpoint}(a) and Table~\ref{tab:checkpoint} sweep the checkpoint interval $k$.
Signature counts and bytes follow the analytic model $(\lfloor n/k\rfloor+1)\cdot|\sigma|$ exactly in all
18 configuration--interval cells: with ML-DSA-65, 135,669\,B (41 signatures) at $k{=}1$, 29,781\,B at
$k{=}5$, 9,927\,B at $k{=}20$, and 3,309\,B at $k{=}\infty$; with ECDSA, 2,912\,B down to 72\,B. Exposure grows
as bytes fall: the client displays at most 5, 25, 100, and 200 tokens before a verified signature covers
them. The corresponding longest verification lags are 0\,ms at $k{=}1$, 0.5--0.8\,s at $k{=}5$, 2.7--6.0\,s at
$k{=}20$, and 5.4--6.6\,s at $k{=}\infty$, where the whole response is unverified until its last record. The
checkpoint interval is therefore a dial between signature bytes and how long a user reads unverified
text; Section~\ref{sec:res-campaign} shows what it buys against an attacker.

exposure for 200-token responses; the measurements lie on the analytic model. (b) Attack campaign on
100-token streams (pooled over six configurations, 3,000 trials per point): tokens displayed with no
verified signature covering them when the client rejected the attack.}

\subsection{Signing Cost Inside a Stream}\label{sec:timing}
Signature \emph{bytes} match the model exactly, but per-signature \emph{time} inside a stream does not
match a back-to-back microbenchmark, and in an earlier version of this paper it appeared inconsistent: the
$k{=}1$ checkpoint cell cost 5.7\,ms of signing and verification for Full PQC but 27.3\,ms for Hybrid, whose
ECDSA signatures are the cheaper ones, and the implied cost per signature varied six-fold across $k$.
Table~\ref{tab:timing} explains why. Signed back to back with the CPU idle, ECDSA P-256 costs
20\,\textmu s and ML-DSA-65 73\,\textmu s; signed once every 125\,ms---the spacing of 5-token
chunks---they cost 343 and 519\,\textmu s. Thread-CPU time rises with wall time in every pattern, so the
extra cost is work the processor executes, not time spent waiting for the interpreter lock or for the
model's thread. Keeping the core busy during the same 125\,ms gaps removes most of it (56 and
96\,\textmu s), and confining the thread to the efficiency cores reproduces most of it (132 and
386\,\textmu s): between chunks the core clocks down or the thread migrates to a slower core, and each
signature then runs slowly. Inside real streams, the per-signature CPU cost of every streaming and
checkpoint cell lies between the back-to-back and the spaced costs: 39--360\,\textmu s for ECDSA and
92--640\,\textmu s for ML-DSA-65, with 100\% and 95\% of cells within 20\% of those bounds. Signing time in a stream is thus
set largely by the processor's power state, which differs from run to run and between strategies with
different signing rhythms; it is bounded, not predicted, by the microbenchmark. In absolute terms it is
small: at most 23\,ms of signing per 200-token stream that takes 5--6\,s to generate.

\input{tables/tab_timing}

\subsection{Stream Integrity Under Attack}\label{sec:res-campaign}
Table~\ref{tab:campaign} reports the campaign: 144,000 attacked trials and 300 unmodified streams,
plus the 450 streams of the streaming sweeps. No unmodified stream was rejected (0/750; 95\% upper bound
0.4\%). Every static attack was detected in every trial and cell (3,000/3,000 each; 95\% lower bound
99.88\%). Per-chunk signing catches drop, reorder, duplication, and replay at the affected chunk, so no
unverified text is shown; the exception is dropping the final chunk (5\% of drops), which only the end
record reveals. A replayed chunk or session fails AEAD decryption under this session's key at once.

\emph{Detection is not prevention.} Without checkpoints, hash-chain signing detects drop, reorder, and
duplication only at the end of the stream, by which time the client has displayed the entire 100-token
response unverified (19--21 chunks). Truncation is detected by every strategy only when the stream ends
without its signed terminal record; with $k{=}\infty$ the client has by then shown on average half the
response (10.4 chunks) without any signature covering it. Checkpoints bound this: the unverified text
shown at rejection falls to 8--9, 3--4, and 0.5 chunks at $k=10$, 5, and 2
(Fig.~\ref{fig:checkpoint}(b)), and every adaptive attack on checkpoints---moving a checkpoint
signature, dropping a chunk next to a checkpoint, reordering across one---is caught at the next
checkpoint. One adaptive attack succeeds against a natural but incomplete client: \emph{stripping every
checkpoint signature} leaves a stream whose content is genuine and whose terminal signature verifies,
so a client that does not check for the checkpoints it requested accepts it (0/3,000 detected in each
cell) while silently losing all mid-stream assurance. Enforcing the requested schedule---a missing
checkpoint is a failure---detects it at the first missing checkpoint in every trial. The results were
identical across all six configurations: detection depends on where signatures fall, not on the
signature scheme.

\input{tables/tab_campaign}

\subsection{Key Substitution and Authenticated Handshakes}\label{sec:res-keysub}
Against the default, unauthenticated handshake, key substitution succeeded in all 1,800 trials
(Table~\ref{tab:keysub}): the adversary read every request and every forged prediction was accepted, in
every configuration, post-quantum or not. Post-quantum key establishment protects recorded traffic from
a future CRQC; it does nothing against an active adversary if the client cannot tell whose keys it
received. With the transcript signature checked under a pinned identity key, all 3,600 substitution
attempts (with the server's transcript signature left in place or replaced by one under the adversary's
own identity key) were rejected at the handshake, before any request was sent, and no unattacked
transaction was rejected. A relayed handshake with a flipped response bit was rejected by the AEAD check
in both modes. Authentication cost little (Table~\ref{tab:authcost}): one extra signature per handshake
(71\,B with ECDSA, 3,309\,B with ML-DSA-65) and a client verification of 86\,\textmu s (ECDSA) or
46\,\textmu s (ML-DSA-65); end-to-end differences at 10 connections were within $\pm1.7$\,ms with
confidence intervals that include zero for every configuration.

\input{tables/tab_keysub}

\input{tables/tab_authcost}

\subsection{Tampering With Single Responses}\label{sec:res-mitm}
Every tampered response was rejected in every configuration (Table~\ref{tab:threats}). A flipped
ciphertext bit is caught by the AES-GCM tag in 0.007--0.009\,ms (median), before the signature is
examined; a flipped signature bit is caught by verification in 0.058--0.059\,ms (ML-DSA-65) and
0.063--0.083\,ms (ECDSA P-256). This shows that the checks work and are cheap; it does not, by itself,
show resistance to a man-in-the-middle (Section~\ref{sec:res-keysub}).

\input{tables/tab_threats}

\subsection{Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Exposure}\label{sec:res-hndl}
A passive adversary captures 209--433\,B per classical transaction and 1,265--4,535\,B per
post-quantum transaction (Fig.~\ref{fig:wirebytes}). Under the modeled attack only the classical
captures---RSA-OAEP and X25519 alike---become decryptable. Under streaming (Fig.~\ref{fig:streaminghndl})
the decryptable volume $D$ grows linearly with response length for both classical key exchanges, at 11.4
bytes per generated token ($R^2{=}0.9997$, 50--585 tokens, one model and tokenizer), of which 5.8 bytes
per token are plaintext and the rest per-chunk AEAD framing. All four ML-KEM configurations have zero
decryptable bytes at every length. These are byte volumes under a modeled key recovery, not measures of
information content.

captures are not decryptable by a future CRQC under the modeled attack; the smaller classical ones are.}

\end{figure}

\subsection{Key Establishment Under Concurrency}\label{sec:res-concurrency}
Table~\ref{tab:concurrency} and Fig.~\ref{fig:concurrency} summarize the sweep; differences are
medians with 95\% two-stage bootstrap CIs. At 10 connections---the setting least affected by the shared
host---the matched-protocol control (Control-2RT) costs $+1.7$\,ms [$-0.9$, $+4.0$] over the control, and
the cryptographic overhead (protected minus Control-2RT) is $+1.3$\,ms [$-0.4$, $+3.7$] for Full PQC,
$+2.3$ [$+0.3$, $+5.0$] for Hybrid, $+2.7$ [$+0.6$, $+5.2$] for Classical-ECDHE, $+4.2$ [$+1.9$, $+7.1$] for
Hybrid-KEX-PQ, $+5.4$ [$+3.2$, $+7.8$] for Hybrid-KEX, and $+76.8$\,ms [$+67.3$, $+89.5$] for Classical-RSA,
against a 92\,ms transaction. All four ML-KEM configurations are equivalent to the X25519 baseline within
$\pm5\%$ at 10 connections (Table~\ref{tab:equivalence}). This confirms, for inference payloads, what
post-quantum TLS studies found for generic traffic~\cite{paquin2020benchmarking,sikeridis2020authentication}:
replacing X25519 with ML-KEM-768 adds no practically significant computation. Classical-RSA's overhead sits
in the handshake, where the server generates a fresh RSA-2048 key pair (Fig.~\ref{fig:decomposition}).

At 1,000 connections, which on a single host is a stress test of client and server contention, the
non-RSA protected configurations take 18.9--20.5\,s against 9.4\,s for the control---but Control-2RT takes
21.3\,s, so the doubling comes from the second HTTP request, not the cryptography; against Control-2RT
the protected configurations are $0.8$--$2.4$\,s \emph{faster}, an artifact of contention rather than a
cryptographic effect. Hybrid ($-1.7\%$ [$-3.7$, $+0.4$]) and Full PQC ($-0.4\%$ [$-1.9$, $+1.0$]) are equivalent
to Classical-ECDHE; Hybrid-KEX ($+2.6\%$ [$-1.2$, $+8.2$]) is not shown equivalent, and Hybrid-KEX-PQ is
faster ($-5.4\%$ [$-8.5$, $-0.8$]). Classical-RSA reaches 30.7\,s.

\paragraph*{Failed requests} At 1,000 connections 1.2--1.6\% of protected requests failed, against 0.2\%
for Control-2RT and none for the control (Table~\ref{tab:failures}). Every failure was a connection reset
(httpx \texttt{ReadError}); none was a timeout or an HTTP error, so the excluded requests were not slow
requests that timed out. Control-2RT's failures all occurred on its first request, those of the protected
configurations on both requests. Re-counting every failed request at the 30\,s client timeout changed
each cryptographic overhead by at most 0.17\,s and changed no equivalence verdict, so excluding failures does
not bias the conclusions. Below 1,000 connections at most 0.2\% of requests failed.

\paragraph*{100 connections} Here the per-repetition medians of the protected configurations are
bimodal---each repetition settles near either $\approx$1,000\,ms or $\approx$1,550\,ms (e.g.\ Classical-ECDHE
1,014--1,701\,ms, Full PQC 988--1,604\,ms; Hybrid-KEX-PQ stayed in the slower mode in all five,
1,562--1,626\,ms)---while both controls are stable (Control-2RT 982--1,003\,ms). We attribute the regime
switching to queueing with client and server on one CPU and do not rank configurations at this level;
only Classical-RSA ($+1.39$\,s over Control-2RT) is clearly separated.

\subsection{Payload Shape}\label{sec:res-payload}
Across the four profiles the cryptographic overhead is roughly constant in absolute terms
(Fig.~\ref{fig:payload}, Table~\ref{tab:payload}): +4.0--9.4\,ms for every non-RSA configuration and
+71.6--110.2\,ms for Classical-RSA. In relative terms it ranges from +4.5\% for the 89\,ms
RandomForest to up to +240\% for millisecond-scale synthetic profiles. The cost of protection is thus an
additive term independent of payload size; whether it matters depends on the inference time it is
added to. Configurations using X25519 (Classical-ECDHE, Hybrid-KEX) are consistently 1.6--3.5\,ms
slower than those using ML-KEM alone, matching the primitive costs: server-side handshake work is
217.9\,\textmu s for X25519 key generation plus exchange against 23.3\,\textmu s for ML-KEM key
generation plus decapsulation in our implementation.

\subsection{Network Conditions}\label{sec:res-network}
On emulated paths (Fig.~\ref{fig:network}) the handshake leg isolates the cost of key-exchange size.
Relative to Classical-ECDHE, the ML-KEM configurations add $+4.6\pm0.5$\,ms (Hybrid),
$+4.7\pm0.3$\,ms (Full PQC), and $+5.7\pm1.3$\,ms (Hybrid-KEX) on the mobile path, and at most
1.0\,ms on the metro and WAN paths. End-to-end, these differences are smaller than the
between-repetition variability of server queueing (standard deviation 15--26\,ms on WAN and mobile),
so they are not resolvable at the application level. Classical-RSA's handshake is 61--81\,ms slower
than Classical-ECDHE's on every path because of key generation, not bytes. Because the proxy does not
model TCP slow start or loss, these are lower bounds.

\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_network_conditions.pdf}
\caption{Emulated network paths (10 connections; mean of five per-repetition medians, error bars one
standard deviation). (a) Handshake round trip. (b) Added handshake time of the ML-KEM configurations

\label{fig:network}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Session Reuse}\label{sec:res-amortization}
Fig.~\ref{fig:amortization} reports overhead versus the control as one key exchange serves $N$
requests. Classical-RSA's +101.2\% at $N{=}1$ disappears at $N{=}10$ ($-1.1\pm1.0$\%). For the other
configurations the overhead falls from +4.0--7.0\% at $N{=}1$ to between $-0.2$ and $+2.1$\% at
$N{=}100$; one intermediate point (Full PQC at $N{=}10$, $+9.0\pm8.4$\%) reflects a single outlying
repetition. For deployments that reuse sessions, post-quantum key establishment cost at most about 2\%
end-to-end in this workload.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_handshake_amortization.pdf}
\caption{Session reuse at 10 connections (mean $\pm$ one standard deviation over five repetitions).
(a) All configurations: Classical-RSA's overhead vanishes once a key exchange serves ten requests.
(b) Zoom without Classical-RSA: post-quantum overhead falls to 0--2\% at 100 requests per key exchange.}
\label{fig:amortization}
\end{figure*}

\section{Ground-Truth Validation}\label{sec:validation}
All 130 tested NIST ACVP known-answer vectors pass (Table~\ref{tab:acvp_results}). Our ML-KEM-768 key
generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation, and our ML-DSA-65 key generation (public and secret key) and
signing (15 deterministic and 15 hedged vectors, external interface with context strings) reproduce the
published outputs byte for byte, and ML-DSA-65 verification returns the expected verdict on every tested
vector. For key generation and signing, liboqs drew exactly the 32 random bytes FIPS~204 specifies and no
others, so the comparison covers the full computation. This checks the correctness of our bindings on these
vectors; it is not ACVP certification, and it covers only the external, pure ML-DSA interface that liboqs
implements.

Signature-count and signature-byte predictions of the analytic model matched the harness exactly for
the three strategies and for all 18 checkpoint cells (for example 41 ML-DSA-65 signatures, 135,669\,B,
at $k{=}1$). For signing \emph{time}, the model gives bounds rather than a prediction: per-signature cost
in a stream lies between the back-to-back and the spaced microbenchmark (Section~\ref{sec:timing}). A
separate, smaller effect is a one-time cost: ECDSA P-256's first signing call in a fresh process took
7.7--9.3\,ms (lazy OpenSSL initialization), which the discarded warm-up generation absorbs.

\section{Discussion and Decision Summary}\label{sec:discussion}
An earlier version of this paper combined an ordinal security score with a latency overhead into one
weighted number. We no longer do so: the two have no common unit, the security score was assigned rather
than derived, and the overhead it used (versus the single-request control) was dominated by the extra
HTTP round trip that Control-2RT shows is not cryptographic. Table~\ref{tab:dominance} instead states three
yes/no security properties of each construction and its measured costs, and asks only which
configurations no other configuration beats on every axis at once. Whatever weights a reader attaches to
the axes, the preferred configuration lies in that non-dominated set.

\input{tables/tab_dominance}

The result is sharper than a ranking. Classical-RSA is dominated (by Classical-ECDHE, and for per-chunk
streaming also by Hybrid-KEX): it is slower and no more secure. No other configuration dominates another.
Latency does not separate them---at 10 connections every non-RSA configuration is within the
equivalence margin of the others or within a few milliseconds of them, and at 1,000 connections the
differences are contention noise---so every step up in security is paid for in \emph{bytes}, not time:
ML-KEM adds about 1\,kB to the handshake, ML-DSA-65 about 3.2\,kB per signature, and with per-chunk
streaming about 133\,kB per 200-token response. Which non-dominated configuration to choose therefore
depends on which security properties a deployment needs and on how many signatures it sends, not on
latency. This is also why the earlier composite score favoured Full PQC: it weighted a security score
that Full PQC maximizes against a latency term that barely varies.

\paragraph*{Hypotheses} \textbf{H1} (bounded post-quantum overhead) is supported at 10 connections, where
all four ML-KEM configurations are equivalent to Classical-ECDHE within $\pm5\%$ and their cryptographic
overhead over the matched protocol is 1.3--5.4\,ms; at 1,000 connections, a single-host stress test, Hybrid
and Full PQC are again equivalent, and at 100 connections queueing bimodality prevents a conclusion.
\textbf{H2} (Hybrid captures Full PQC's HNDL benefit at lower cost) is supported on HNDL, where both have
zero decryptable bytes under the modeled attack; on cost it holds only for signature bytes, which matter
when many signatures are sent. \textbf{H3} (categorically different decryptability) is demonstrated:
classical exposure grows linearly with streamed tokens, ML-KEM-based exposure stays at zero.
\textbf{H4} (ML-DSA-65 does not slow responses) needs restating. ML-DSA-65 \emph{verification} is faster than
ECDSA P-256 (28,202 versus 21,602 per second), but verification is the client's cost; the server's cost is
\emph{signing}, where ML-DSA-65 is 3.2$\times$ slower (67.9 versus 21.0\,\textmu s median). That difference,
about 47\,\textmu s per response back to back and about 180\,\textmu s per signature in the spaced
pattern of a stream, is under 0.2\% of a 92\,ms transaction and is not resolvable end to end
(Table~\ref{tab:concurrency}). H4 holds on that basis, not on verification speed.

% =============================================================================
\section{Recommendations}

These follow from our measurements under our threat model; each is a design choice for an
application-layer protocol, not a statement about TLS stacks.

\paragraph*{Authenticate the handshake} Post-quantum key establishment does not stop an active
adversary who substitutes keys; only authentication of the server's keys does
(Section~\ref{sec:res-keysub}). Sign the handshake transcript with an identity key the client can verify
(in TLS, a certificate and CertificateVerify), using ML-DSA-65 where quantum-resistant authentication is
required. In our measurements this cost one signature per handshake and no resolvable latency.

\paragraph*{Key establishment} Within the modeled threat, replacing X25519 with ML-KEM-768 removes the HNDL
key-recovery exposure at no practically significant computational cost (equivalent within $\pm5\%$ at 10
connections), about 5\,ms of handshake time on a slow emulated link (a lower bound), and 0--2\% once
sessions are reused. Where hedging against an ML-KEM weakness matters, X25519MLKEM768 cost about 3\,ms more
than ML-KEM alone at 10 connections. Per-handshake RSA key generation should be avoided: it occupied 4--5
CPU cores at modest load.

\paragraph*{Signatures} For single responses, choose the signature by the required security property,
not by latency: ML-DSA-65 signing costs about 47\,\textmu s more per response than ECDSA P-256, which was
not measurable end to end, while its 3,309\,B signature adds bytes to every response.

\paragraph*{Streaming} Use hash-chained signing with checkpoints, bind role, session, and position into
every signed message, end every stream with a signed length record, and have the client enforce the
checkpoint schedule it requested (Section~\ref{sec:res-campaign}). Choose $k$ from the exposure the
application can tolerate: $k{=}\infty$ (one signature; the response is unverified until it ends) only where
unverified text is harmless, small $k$ where a user must not act on it. With ML-DSA-65, $k{=}5$ bounds
exposure to 25 tokens for 29,781\,B per 200-token response, against 135,669\,B for per-chunk signing.
Remember that detection is not prevention: a client should mark text as unverified until a signature
covers it, and withdraw it if verification fails. Buffer-and-sign is justified only when chunk-count and
timing metadata must be hidden~\cite{weiss2024keylogging}, at a 40$\times$ time-to-first-token penalty.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Recommendation summary}
\label{tab:recommendations}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}L{2.9cm}L{4.9cm}@{}}
\toprule
Scenario & Recommendation \\
\midrule
Any protected API & Authenticate the handshake (transcript signature under a trusted identity key) \\
Key establishment & ML-KEM-768, or X25519MLKEM768 to hedge against an ML-KEM break \\
Single responses & ECDSA P-256 or ML-DSA-65 by required security; latency does not decide \\
Streaming, display-only & Hash-chain, large $k$; mark text unverified until covered \\
Streaming, actionable output & Hash-chain with small $k$ (e.g.\ $k=5$: 25-token exposure) \\
Any streaming & Bind session context; signed end record; enforce the checkpoint schedule \\
Quantum-resistant authenticity & ML-DSA-65 (Full PQC or Hybrid-KEX-PQ) \\
Metadata-sensitive streaming & Buffer-and-sign \\
Legacy RSA key transport & Migrate away \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\section{Limitations and Threats to Validity}\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph*{Internal validity}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Single host, shared CPU.} All measurements come from one Apple M3 laptop on which the load
  generator and the server share the CPU. This matters most at high concurrency: at 1,000 connections
  both the protected configurations and Control-2RT are dominated by contention, and at 100 connections
  the protected configurations switch between two latency regimes across repetitions while both controls
  do not. We therefore rank configurations only at 10 and 1,000 connections, treat 1,000 connections as a
  single-host stress test, and regard the 10-connection results as the most reliable. A separate
  load-generator host would remove this confound; we did not have one.
  \item \textbf{Failed requests.} At 1,000 connections 0.2--1.6\% of requests failed, all as connection
  resets. Excluding them could bias latency toward configurations that fail more; the sensitivity
  analysis in Section~\ref{sec:res-concurrency} counts each failure at the client timeout instead.
  \item \textbf{Processor power state.} Per-signature time inside a stream depends on how far the core
  has clocked down between chunks (Section~\ref{sec:timing}); on a busy server it would be closer to the
  back-to-back microbenchmark. We report wall-clock and CPU time and give both bounds, and we compare
  signature \emph{bytes}, which are exact, rather than signing times across strategies.
  \item \textbf{Thermal drift.} Generation slowed from $\approx$40 to $\approx$33 tokens/s during streaming
  sweeps on the fanless host. Cell order was shuffled within each configuration, so strategy comparisons
  are unbiased, but streaming times are not compared across configurations.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph*{Construct validity}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Application-layer emulation, not TLS.} PQ-Shield reproduces the cryptographic work of a
  protected transaction with a purpose-built protocol: no TLS framing, record layer, PKI, or TLS
  resumption (PSK, 0-RTT). Its default fresh key exchange per transaction is a worst case;
  Section~\ref{sec:sessions} measures the amortized case. The default handshake is unauthenticated, so
  the default configurations are not resistant to key substitution
  (Section~\ref{sec:res-keysub}); the authenticated variant pins one identity key and does not model
  certificate chains.
  \item \textbf{Byte-level network emulation.} The proxy models propagation delay and bandwidth but not
  slow start, the initial congestion window, loss, or fragmentation, so network costs are lower bounds;
  packet-level studies~\cite{paquin2020benchmarking,sikeridis2020authentication} remain the reference.
  \item \textbf{HNDL measures bytes, not information.} $D$ counts ciphertext bytes that become decryptable
  under the modeled attack; it does not measure what an adversary learns from them, and the per-token rate
  depends on chunk size and tokenizer. Response length leaks without a CRQC~\cite{weiss2024keylogging}.
  \item \textbf{Attack trials sample positions.} Campaign trials replay attacks on captured streams at
  random positions; they cover the attack space but are not independent network events, and they test the
  attacks listed, not every possible adversary.
  \item \textbf{Classical-RSA is a worst case.} Per-handshake RSA-2048 key generation does not reflect
  production practice; Classical-ECDHE is the realistic classical baseline.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph*{External validity}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{One host class and one model.} Results come from Apple silicon with OpenSSL and liboqs;
  server-class x86 CPUs, other libraries, and GPU-served models may differ in absolute terms. Streaming
  uses one quantized 3B-parameter model.
  \item \textbf{Workloads.} The concurrency experiments use a RandomForest classifier; the
  \texttt{image\_cnn} profile is an untrained fixed-weight network and the \texttt{embedding} and
  \texttt{llm\_completion} profiles are synthetic. They probe payload shape and size, not model
  behaviour, so the absolute overheads should be read against the inference time of the target workload.
  \item \textbf{Coverage of C$'$.} Hybrid-KEX-PQ was added in revision and is absent from the payload,
  network, and session-reuse sweeps; Hybrid-KEX's concurrency data come from a supplementary run on the
  same host and day.
  \item \textbf{Side channels.} We did not evaluate constant-time behaviour or cache-timing leakage of the
  bindings or the streaming verification path.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph*{Statistical conclusion validity} Five repetitions per cell bound the precision of
between-run comparisons: with repetition medians as the unit, the smallest attainable $p$ is 0.008, and
equivalence can be shown only for differences well inside the $\pm5\%$ margin.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
For a streamed LLM response, the post-quantum cost lies in the signature schedule, not the key exchange.
Per-chunk ML-DSA-65 signing adds 135,669\,B to a 200-token response; one terminal signature adds 3,309\,B
but leaves the whole response unverified until it ends. A hash chain checkpointed every $k$ chunks spans
that range with signature bytes that follow an analytic model exactly. Binding role, session, and
position into every signed message, ending each stream with a signed length record, and enforcing the
requested checkpoint schedule made every one of the attacks we tested detectable, including truncation
and checkpoint stripping. Detection, however, arrives only when a signature does, and $k$ sets how much
unverified text a user has seen by then. The answers to the practical questions follow; each holds under
our threat model and on our single host.

\paragraph*{Strongest security} Hybrid-KEX-PQ (X25519MLKEM768 with ML-DSA-65) is the only evaluated
configuration with all three properties we track: key establishment that resists a CRQC, key establishment
that survives an ML-KEM break, and quantum-resistant signatures. Full PQC lacks only the hedge. Neither
resists key substitution unless the handshake is authenticated.

\paragraph*{Best performance} There is no single fastest configuration. At 10 connections every ML-KEM
configuration is equivalent to X25519 within $\pm5\%$, with cryptographic overheads of 1.3--5.4\,ms per
92\,ms transaction; only Classical-RSA with per-transaction key generation is clearly slower. When many
signatures are sent, the ECDSA-signed configurations are cheapest in bytes, by about 47$\times$ per
signature.

\paragraph*{Best balance} Classical-RSA is dominated; among the rest, no configuration is better on every
axis, and moving up in security costs bytes rather than latency. For non-streaming APIs and for streaming
with few signatures, Full PQC or Hybrid-KEX-PQ gives the strongest security for a few kilobytes per
response. When every chunk must be signed or checkpoints are frequent, Hybrid or Hybrid-KEX keeps
signatures at $\approx$2.9\,kB instead of 136\,kB per 200 tokens, at the price of classical signatures.

\paragraph*{What the answer depends on} \emph{Streaming:} the number of signatures, through $k$, sets the
post-quantum cost and the exposure. \emph{Session reuse:} one key exchange per 100 requests reduced every
non-RSA configuration's overhead to 0--2\%. \emph{Threat model:} HNDL confidentiality needs ML-KEM; active
attacks need an authenticated handshake; quantum-resistant authenticity needs ML-DSA-65; hedging against an
ML-KEM break needs the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid. \emph{Network:} slow links add a few milliseconds of
handshake time for ML-KEM, more under packet loss than our byte-level emulation shows.

Future work includes a separate load-generator host and server-class hardware, packet-level network
emulation, a TLS-native implementation with certificate chains and resumption, mid-stream rekeying to
bound HNDL exposure per session, larger models and real request traces, other tokenizers for the HNDL
rate, and constant-time and side-channel analysis of the streaming verification path.
